subChunks.title: SELECT, FROM, WHERE
subChunks.hookHtml: Three words power 80% of all SQL ever written: SELECT, FROM, and WHERE. Master them and you can retrieve any single fact from any table.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The basic shape

SELECT columns
FROM   table
WHERE  condition;

SELECT — choose columns

SELECT * FROM apprentices;          -- all columns
SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices;   -- two columns
SELECT name AS wizard FROM apprentices;  -- rename with AS

In production, list columns explicitly rather than using * — it makes queries resilient to schema changes.

WHERE — filter rows

SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices WHERE xp >= 2000;
SELECT *          FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Mage';
SELECT name       FROM apprentices WHERE id = 3;

Without WHERE every row is returned. With it, only rows satisfying the condition are returned.

String literals need single quotes

'Mage' not "Mage". Double quotes in standard SQL refer to identifiers (column names), not string values. Always single-quote strings.

Comparison operators

= <> != < <= > >= — all work as expected.

storyBeats.text: Cipher slides the ledger toward you and places a quill in your hand.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: SELECT — the columns you want. FROM — the table they live in. WHERE — the filter. Three words, and you can answer almost anything the Headmaster asks of these archives.

storyBeats.speaker: Finding Mages
storyBeats.text:
SELECT name, xp
FROM   apprentices
WHERE  rank = 'Mage';
-- Returns only rows where rank equals 'Mage'

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 First query

The Headmaster wants the name and xp of every apprentice with at least 2 000 XP. Write the query.

-- Data loaded:
-- id | name    | rank        | xp
--  1 | Alice   | Apprentice  | 1200
--  2 | Bjorn   | Adept       | 2400
--  3 | Cassia  | Mage        | 4800
--  4 | Dorian  | Novice      |   80
--  5 | Elara   | Archmage    | 7500
--  6 | Fenrir  | Apprentice  |  950
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
SELECT
  -- columns here
FROM apprentices
WHERE
  -- condition here
;

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what SELECT, FROM, and WHERE each do, and why single-quoting strings matters in SQL.

questions.prompt: What does the WHERE clause do in a SELECT query?
options: Filters rows so only those matching the condition are returned
Picks which columns appear in the result
Specifies which table to read from
questions.answer: Filters rows so only those matching the condition are returned
questions.explanation: SELECT chooses columns; FROM chooses the table; WHERE filters rows. Sorting is handled by ORDER BY (next lesson).

questions.prompt: Using the lesson data, what does `SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE xp >= 2000` return?
questions.explanation: Bjorn (2400), Cassia (4800), and Elara (7500) all have xp >= 2000. Alice (1200), Dorian (80), and Fenrir (950) do not.

questions.prompt: Which query correctly returns all columns for the apprentice named 'Alice'?
options: SELECT ALL FROM apprentices WHERE name IS 'Alice';
questions.explanation: Single quotes denote string literals in standard SQL. `SELECT *` returns all columns. The other options use double quotes (identifiers), non-standard IS, or are missing the FROM clause.

questions.prompt: Why does `SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = "Mage"` fail in strict SQL engines?
options: Double quotes denote identifiers in standard SQL, so the engine looks for a column named Mage rather than the string 'Mage'
Double quotes are reserved for integers
The WHERE clause cannot filter on TEXT columns
SELECT needs a semicolon before WHERE
questions.answer: Double quotes denote identifiers in standard SQL, so the engine looks for a column named Mage rather than the string 'Mage'
questions.explanation: Standard SQL: single quotes = string literals; double quotes = identifiers (table/column names). Many engines tolerate double-quoted strings, but writing single quotes is the portable, correct habit.
